relations.myth: The heavenly court and Job’s testing
relations.note: YHWH praises Job and permits the accuser to test him under limits.

relations.myth: YHWH answers Job from the whirlwind
relations.note: YHWH confronts Job with creation’s vastness without explaining his suffering.

relations.myth: Job’s fortunes and family are restored
relations.note: YHWH accepts Job’s intercession and restores his prosperity and family.

relations.myth: The heavenly challenge and two tests
relations.note: The accuser challenges Job’s piety and inflicts losses, bereavement, and disease.
The Hebrew book presents an unnamed woman as Job’s wife.

relations.myth: Job’s wife urges him to curse God
relations.note: She urges Job to bless or curse God and die; Job rebukes her.

relations.myth: Job disputes retribution with Eliphaz
relations.note: Eliphaz consoles, accuses, and debates Job about suffering and divine justice.

relations.myth: Job intercedes for the rebuked friends
relations.note: Job prays for Eliphaz after YHWH orders sacrifice and intercession.

relations.myth: Job disputes retribution with Bildad
relations.note: Bildad debates Job, defends traditional retribution, and implicates Job’s dead children.

relations.myth: Job intercedes for the rebuked friends
relations.note: Job’s prayer accompanies Bildad’s required closing sacrifice.

relations.myth: Job disputes retribution with Zophar
relations.note: Zophar debates Job and claims that Job deserves still greater punishment.

relations.myth: Job intercedes for the rebuked friends
relations.note: Job’s prayer accompanies Zophar’s required closing sacrifice.

relations.other: Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite
relations.myth: Elihu rebukes Job and the friends
relations.note: Elihu attacks Job’s claims and argues that suffering can discipline or instruct.
Jemimah is Job’s restored daughter and receives an inheritance.
Keziah is Job’s restored daughter and receives an inheritance.
Keren-happuch is Job’s restored daughter and receives an inheritance.

relations.myth: YHWH displays Behemoth to Job
relations.note: Behemoth is shown as a mighty creature beyond Job’s mastery.

relations.myth: YHWH challenges Job concerning Leviathan
relations.note: Job is challenged to capture or domesticate Leviathan but never encounters it.

relations.myth: Three exemplary righteous men
relations.note: Job and Noah appear together as proverbial righteous men without meeting.

relations.myth: Three exemplary righteous men
relations.note: Job and Daniel or Danel appear jointly in Ezekiel’s righteous triad.

relations.myth: Greek appendix identifies Job as Jobab
relations.note: The Septuagint appendix equates Job with the Edomite king Jobab.
The Septuagint appendix makes Zare or Zerah the father of Jobab-Job.
The Septuagint appendix places Job within Esau’s Edomite lineage.
The Septuagint genealogy makes Job fifth in descent from Abraham through Esau.
Several later Jewish traditions make Jacob’s daughter Dinah Job’s wife.
relations.source: Pseudo-Philo; Testament of Job; Genesis Rabbah

relations.note: Job becomes Jacob’s son-in-law when later tradition identifies his wife as Dinah.

relations.myth: Pharaoh’s advisers debate Israelite oppression
relations.note: Rabbinic legend makes Job and Balaam fellow advisers in Pharaoh’s court.

relations.myth: Pharaoh’s advisers debate Israelite oppression
relations.note: Jethro opposes Pharaoh and flees, contrasting with Job’s alleged silence.

relations.myth: Job placed in the time of Moses
relations.note: One rabbinic strand makes Job Moses’ contemporary and says Moses wrote his book.

relations.myth: Job destroys Satan’s idol
relations.note: Job destroys Satan’s idol, and Satan retaliates through disguises and disasters.
The Testament names Sitis or Sitidos as Job’s first wife.

relations.myth: Sitis sustains Job during Satan’s attack
relations.note: Sitis supports Job, sells her hair for bread, and dies after lamenting.

relations.myth: Job gives his daughters heavenly cords
relations.note: Job gives them supernatural cords enabling angelic speech and celestial hymnody.
Patristic exegesis treats Job as a type of Christ rather than a companion.

relations.myth: Ayyūb prays and receives healing
relations.note: Allah removes Ayyūb’s distress, provides healing water, and restores his family.

relations.myth: Allah commends Ayyūb’s patience
relations.note: Allah praises Ayyūb as patient and an excellent servant.

relations.myth: Iblīs instigates Ayyūb’s affliction
relations.note: Later Islamic stories make Iblīs personally cause Ayyūb’s losses and disease.
Post-Qurʾānic narratives commonly name Ayyūb’s faithful wife Raḥma.

relations.myth: Ayyūb fulfills his oath with a bundle
relations.note: Later exegesis says Ayyūb symbolically strikes his wife without violating his oath.

relations.myth: Gabriel brings guidance or relief to Ayyūb
relations.note: Some later Islamic narratives make Gabriel the bearer of divine guidance or relief.
